hints: Focus on what hot concentrated sulfuric acid does to an alcohol, it removes water to make a C=C double bond in every possible position.
Look at carbon 3 where the OH is, and list the three different neighbouring carbons that can lose a hydrogen: C2, C4 and the methyl group on C3.
Now check each new alkene for E/Z stereoisomerism by seeing if both ends of the double bond carry two different groups.
walkthrough:
**Identify the reaction as dehydration**

This is elimination of water from an alcohol to form alkenes. The OH leaves from C3, and an H is removed from an adjacent carbon.

$$\text{C}_7\text{H}_{15}\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{C}_7\text{H}_{14} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Find the three different structural alkene skeletons**

Draw $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{-C(OH)(CH}_3\text{)-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. C3 is joined to three carbons with H atoms: C2 ($\text{CH}_2$), C4 ($\text{CH}_2$) and the $\text{CH}_3$ branch.

Loss of H from C2 gives $\text{3-methylhex-2-ene}$. Loss of H from C4 gives $\text{3-methylhex-3-ene}$. Loss of H from the branch methyl gives $\text{2-ethylpent-1-ene}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$.

**Check each alkene for E/Z stereoisomerism**

For E/Z you need two different groups on each C of the double bond. For $\text{3-methylhex-2-ene}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=C(CH}_3\text{)(CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\text{)}$, both ends are disubstituted differently, so E and Z forms exist: 2 isomers.

For $\text{3-methylhex-3-ene}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C(CH}_3\text{)=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$, both ends are also disubstituted differently, so E and Z forms exist: 2 isomers.

**Add up the total isomers**

The terminal alkene $\text{2-ethylpent-1-ene}$ has $\text{CH}_2\text{=}$ at one end, so no E/Z is possible: 1 isomer.

Total = 2 + 2 + 1 = 5 isomeric alkenes.

options.A: 3 counts only the three structural skeletons and forgets stereoisomerism. Both 3-methylhex-2-ene and 3-methylhex-3-ene can exist as E and Z forms, so the total is larger.
options.B: 4 usually comes from counting E/Z for only one of the internal alkenes. In fact both internal alkenes have two different groups on each end of the double bond, so both show E/Z isomerism.
options.C: 5 is correct: 2 stereoisomers of 3-methylhex-2-ene plus 2 stereoisomers of 3-methylhex-3-ene plus 1 terminal alkene 2-ethylpent-1-ene gives 5 distinct C7H14 products.
options.D: 6 overcounts, often by assuming the terminal alkene also shows E/Z isomerism. With a CH2= group, one end of the double bond has two identical H atoms, so E/Z is impossible.
